source: Wallas (1926) The Art of Thought; Poincare (1910), as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Wallas named the stage where a problem is not consciously worked on 'Incubation', drawing on Poincare's mathematical self-reports. Order: Preparation, Incubation, Illumination (Inspiration), Verification. Wallas also proposed spreading 'associative chains' and an 'Intimation' feeling before the solution arrives.
numbers: No experiment. Based on introspection.
quote: Incubation is proposed as a useful stage after conscious Preparation but preceding Illumination and Verification.
limits: Gilhooly notes Poincare reported his examples nearly 30 years later, and famous cases (Coleridge Kubla Khan, Mozart, Kekule benzene dream) were shown to be false by Weisberg (2006). Read second-hand via Gilhooly's review text.
agent_relevance: The stage model is a descriptive label, not a tested mechanism. Our schema already has explicit explore, impasse and verify states; the only stage with no code counterpart is Incubation.

source: Poincare (1910) via Gilhooly (2016): subliminal self and hooked-atom model
finding: Poincare proposed unconscious combination of ideas like hooked atoms colliding at random after preparation sets them moving; a selection process (sense of mathematical beauty) promotes the good combination to consciousness. He also said unconscious work never delivers a long calculation already done. Campbell (1960) generalised this to blind variation and selective retention.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Domain-narrow (mathematics). Selection mechanism not specified for other fields.
agent_relevance: Maps to generate-many-then-select: blind variation plus a selector. The selector is the hard part, as with an LLM judge.

source: Wagner, Gais, Haider, Verleger, Born (2004) Sleep inspires insight, Nature 427:352-355
finding: In the Number Reduction Task (8-digit strings of 1, 4, 9; two rules; a hidden shortcut where the second response equals the final answer), sleep between training and retest more than doubled the chance of discovering the hidden rule versus wake.
numbers: Main experiment: 8 h interval, 3 training blocks then 10 retest blocks. Sleep group 13/22 (59.1%) gained insight; each wake group (night wake, day wake) 5/22 (22.7%). chi2 = 8.54, d.f. 2, P = 0.014. Time of insight did not differ between groups (sleep 4.5 blocks +/- 0.8 s.e.m.).
quote: More than twice as many subjects gained insight into the hidden rule after sleep as after wakefulness.
limits: Small groups (22 each). Insight is a behavioural shortcut, not self-report. Schonauer 2018 did not extend it to classical insight problems.
agent_relevance: The founding positive result for sleep-aided insight; useful only as background since our agent cannot sleep.

source: Wagner et al. (2004) controls: no-training groups
finding: Sleep helped only when the task had been trained before sleep. Subjects with no initial training who slept or stayed awake gained insight at the wake rate. This points to offline restructuring of an already acquired representation, not a general sleep boost.
numbers: No-training controls: 5/20 (25.0%) gained insight in each of two conditions, versus 59.1% in the sleep group: chi2 = 7.07, d.f. 2, P = 0.029. Sleepers' stage mix: stage 2 58.6%, SWS 17.2%, REM 17.7% (mean).
limits: Tiredness ratings were lower after sleep, but the night-wake and day-wake conditions argue against tiredness and circadian explanations. No stage-specific claim in the paper.
agent_relevance: Insight needs a prior worked representation before the break. A break with no prior attempt (for an agent: no first draft) gave no gain.

source: Wagner et al. (2004): reaction-time antecedents of insight
finding: Later solvers showed distinct reaction-time patterns across the sleep or wake interval, so restructuring seemed to start before the explicit rule was noticed. The authors link it to hippocampus-driven reorganisation during sleep.
numbers: Reaction times fell in both sleep and wake; solver versus non-solver difference marked P < 0.01 and P < 0.001 (exact cell values not extracted).
limits: Mechanism claims (hippocampus, medial temporal lobe) are interpretive and untested directly.
agent_relevance: Suggests insight can follow implicit change; an agent only has visible tokens, so there is no direct analogue.

source: Cai, Mednick, Harrison, Kanady, Mednick (2009) REM, not incubation, improves creativity by priming associative networks, PNAS 106:10130
finding: With Remote Associates Test items primed by morning analogies, a REM nap raised performance on primed items by almost 40% over morning baseline. NREM and quiet rest did not. Repeated items improved equally in all groups (time alone, 'incubation'). New items did not improve in any group.
numbers: N = 77 over two experiments (Exp 1 n=25: REM 10, NREM 6, rest 9; Exp 2 n=52: REM 18, NREM 6, rest 28). Primed items P = 0.04 (text) or 0.047 (caption). Repeated items P = 0.67. New items P = 0.261. Memory tests did not differ (recognition P = 0.283, cued recall 0.353). Total sleep time vs gain r = .104, P = 0.53.
quote: REM enhanced the formation of associative networks and the integration of unassociated information.
limits: NREM n = 6 in each experiment. One task (RAT), young adults. Inconsistent P values between text and caption. Cholinergic mechanism untested.
agent_relevance: Hedges the 'sleep helps' claim: benefit depends on prior exposure and stage. Plain elapsed time helped only for repeated items.

source: Schonauer, Brodt, Pohlchen, Bressmer, Danek, Gais (2018) Sleep does not promote solving classical insight problems and magic tricks, Front Hum Neurosci 12:72
finding: Failed to find a sleep benefit for insight problems. Sessions back-to-back or 3 h apart, spent asleep or awake, with and without incubation. Neither sleep nor incubation changed solving on 10 magic tricks or on matchstick, nine-dot and eight-coin problems.
numbers: N = 77 adults (mean age 23.8), four groups. Magic tricks: sleep F = 0.047, p = 0.829; incubation F = 0.008, p = 0.930; about 1.40 extra tricks solved at retest regardless. Classical problems: sleep F(1,73) = 0.641, p = 0.426; incubation F(1,73) = 0.131, p = 0.719; interaction p = 0.939. About 54% of magic-trick solutions came with sudden insight, unchanged by sleep. Sleep stages did not correlate with performance.
quote: Sleep did not improve solving or subjective insight.
limits: 80% power only for eta-p2 >= 0.1; effects under 1% of variance could not be excluded. Different tasks from Wagner's NRT. They flag that Wagner reported no experimenter-expectancy controls.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the incubation and sleep benefit is task-specific and weak for classical insight problems. Supports leaving Incubation out of the schema.

source: Holda, Glodek, Dankiewicz-Berger, Skrzypinska, Szmigielska (2020) Ill-defined problem solving does not benefit from daytime napping, Front Psychol 11
finding: Nap versus waking control on a long interactive crime-story problem. Napping improved neither solution quality nor creativity (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration), and performance was unrelated to sleep stage or dream reports.
numbers: N = 40, randomised to nap or wake, polysomnography monitored. No effect sizes extracted.
limits: Abstract only via Europe PMC record; full text blocked by captcha.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: realistic ill-defined problems show no nap incubation benefit.

source: Lowe, Petzka, Tzegka, Schuck (2025) N2 sleep promotes the occurrence of 'aha' moments in a perceptual insight task, PLOS Biology 23(6):e3003185
finding: Preregistered 20-minute nap study. Insight into a hidden strategy in a perceptual task was more likely after N2 sleep than after wake. N1 sleep did not raise insight (the preregistered N1 hypothesis failed).
numbers: Recruited N = 90, analysed N = 68. N2 24/28 (85.7%), N1 14/22 (63.6%), wake 10/18 (55.5%). N2 vs wake Fisher p = 0.038; N1 vs wake p = 0.75; N1 vs N2 p = 0.1. Bayes factor N2 > wake 8.19, N2 > N1 24.71. Baseline without nap 49/99 (49.5%).
quote: We thus find no evidence that N1 sleep promotes insight as reported by Lacaux
limits: Sleep stage not randomised; the N2 result is post hoc. Methods list 30 exclusions that do not reconcile with N = 68. No CIs reported.
agent_relevance: Partial support for Wagner, with a stage-specific, quasi-experimental design.

source: Konkoly, Morris, Hurka, Martinez, Sanders, Paller (2026) Creative problem-solving after experimentally provoking dreams of unsolved puzzles during REM sleep, Neuroscience of Consciousness
finding: Frequent lucid dreamers tried puzzles, each paired with a soundtrack. During REM half the soundtracks were replayed (targeted memory reactivation) with an instruction to keep working on the puzzle in the dream. Cues reliably increased dreaming about the puzzles. Post hoc, in those whose cue-related dreaming rose, next-day solving also improved.
numbers: Abstract has no numbers; counts not extracted.
limits: Post hoc subgroup result. Selected population (lucid dreamers). Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Causal test of dreaming-as-incubation; links to the targeted memory reactivation subfield in this run.

source: Sio and Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review, Psychological Bulletin 135:94-120
finding: Pooled 117 studies; overall positive incubation effect, mean d = 0.29 (low to medium). Larger for divergent thinking than for linguistic or visual insight problems. Longer preparation raised the effect. Cognitively demanding activity during the break lowered it. Low-demand activity beat rest for linguistic insight problems.
numbers: d = 0.29 over 117 studies (as reported by Gilhooly 2016; the abstract has no numbers).
limits: Read only second-hand (Gilhooly review text, plus the abstract record). Publication bias not assessed in what I read.
agent_relevance: Break benefit is small. For an agent, a pause means unrelated tokens, so even this small gain is not expected.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and creative problem solving (Frontiers in Psychology 7:1076): Strick et al. (2011) meta-analysis of immediate incubation (decision studies)
finding: For immediate incubation (distraction right after the problem is shown, no prior work), 92 decision studies gave a significant beneficial effect. Moderators: more options, shorter presentation, shorter incubation, configural mindset all raised it.
numbers: g = 0.224 aggregate over 92 studies (as reported by Gilhooly).
limits: Second-hand. Decision studies, not insight problems. The unconscious thought effect is contested (see Steindorf 2021).
agent_relevance: Immediate incubation cannot be explained by forgetting a fixation, since no fixation has formed yet.

source: Segal (2004) Incubation in insight problem solving, Creativity Research Journal 16:141-148, as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Segal used a square-and-parallelogram area problem (restructure into two triangles to make a rectangle). After the solver felt an impasse, a break of 4 or 12 min on a demanding verbal task (crossword) or an undemanding one (browsing newspapers) gave benefits versus no break, but break length and break demand did not matter. Segal's 'Fresh Look' view: simply switching attention away is enough.
numbers: Significant benefit of break vs no break; no effect of 4 vs 12 min or task demand. Sample sizes not in the source I read.
limits: Second-hand description. The task is spatial and the break tasks verbal, so similarity is confounded. Fresh Look predicts no immediate-incubation effect.
agent_relevance: Fresh Look is the cheapest mechanism to emulate: drop the working context and restart. It matches what a fresh sample or context reset does.

source: Smith (1995) and Smith and Blankenship (1991), as described in Gilhooly (2016): beneficial forgetting
finding: With word problems given helpful or misleading cues, solvers who failed and then had a break solved more when they had forgotten the misleading cues, and forgetting grew with break length. Supports fixation decay as an incubation mechanism.
numbers: No numbers in the source I read.
limits: Second-hand. Forgetting cannot explain immediate incubation benefits.
agent_relevance: Fixation on a misleading first approach is real for LLM chains too; the remedy is to remove the wrong approach from context, not to wait.

source: Baird, Smallwood, Mrazek, Kam, Franklin, Schooler (2012) Inspired by distraction: mind wandering facilitates creative incubation, Psychological Science (PMID 22941876)
finding: Unusual Uses Task. An undemanding break that lets the mind wander improved performance on problems seen before, more than a demanding task, rest or no break. The gain tracked rate of mind wandering, not deliberate thoughts about the task.
numbers: Abstract has no digits; sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Gilhooly cites it as ruling out intermittent conscious work. The 2025 preregistered test (next line) found a much weaker pattern.
agent_relevance: An under-demanding break wins; agents have no equivalent of cheap mind wandering.

source: Preregistered 2025 Scientific Reports test of mind wandering during incubation in a writing task (PMC12241419)
finding: Preregistered study, two short stories with a 10-minute break (0-back, 2-back, mindfulness, or no break). No incubation task raised creative improvement overall. Mind wandering predicted improvement only when the same prompt was repeated, and only on semantic-distance (forward flow) and GPT-4 ratings, not human ratings.
numbers: N = 200 recruited (about 125 to 135 analysed). Task effect on mind wandering F(2,129) = 10.8, p < .001. Forward flow beta = 0.33, p = .024; GPT-4 ratings beta = 6.76, p = .036; human ratings beta = -1.39, p = .793. New prompt: p = .495 and .432. Human rater alpha = 0.72; forward flow vs human r(382) = 0.51.
quote: Mind wandering during incubation was assessed with a validated retrospective questionnaire
limits: Correlational. Retrospective questionnaire. Mindfulness gave more mind wandering than 0-back (p = .009), opposite to expectation. Human and automated ratings diverge. Exact title and authors not read from the page.
agent_relevance: Weak, rating-dependent link; also an example of GPT-4 used as a scorer that diverged from human raters.

source: Henok, Vallee-Tourangeau, Vallee-Tourangeau (2018/2020) Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving, Psychological Research (PMC6994426)
finding: Cheap necklace problem, retested after two weeks. Working with manipulable chains (high interactivity) beat pen and paper at time 1, and incubation gains were biggest when time 2 was done in the high-interactivity context.
numbers: Exp 1 N = 63: time 1 high 12/28 (43%) vs low 2/35 (6%), chi2 = 12.42, p < .001; time 2 among non-solvers high 7/16 (44%) vs low 5/33 (15%), p = .029. Exp 2: low-to-high 14/23 (61%) vs high-to-low 1/20 (5%). Mean gains: low-low +14%, low-high +52%, high-low +3%, high-high +25%.
quote: The effect of incubation was strongest when it was realised in a high-interactivity context.
limits: One problem, small mostly female student samples, no no-gap control, so repeat exposure is not separated from incubation. Sample counts vary in the report (61 vs 55).
agent_relevance: The break works only if the later attempt can act on the problem differently (tools, manipulation). For an agent: after a pause give it tools or a new working form, not the same text.

source: Gilhooly et al. (2012, 2013, 2015) as described in Gilhooly (2016): tests of intermittent conscious work and task similarity
finding: Checks for secret conscious work during the break found none: interpolated tasks (mental rotation, anagrams) were not impaired, and correlations between interpolated and later target scores averaged 0.11 (6 of 8 positive). In the Alternative Uses task immediate incubation helped more than delayed. A dissimilar-modality break helped more than a similar one, against forgetting accounts and for unconscious work.
numbers: 8 Pearson correlations, mean r = 0.11, one significant (r = 0.36, p < .05, opposite to prediction). Other sample sizes not in source.
limits: Second-hand. The author is also the reviewer. Alternative explanation: selective fatigue relief (Ellwood 2009).
agent_relevance: A different-modality break suggests that sampling a different style of attempt, not repeating the same one, is what helps.

source: Dijksterhuis and Nordgren (2006) Unconscious Thought Theory; Steindorf, Rummel, Boywitt (2021) A fresh look at the unconscious thought effect
finding: UTT says unconscious thought is parallel, bottom-up, inexact, divergent, and best for complex decisions. A 2021 analysis of 822 participants over three experiments on apartment evaluation found the effect only in the first two, and its link to less deliberation vanished once thoughts were probed during the filler.
numbers: 822 participants, three experiments (Steindorf 2021 abstract via Europe PMC).
limits: Abstract-level for Steindorf; UTT description via Gilhooly. Other UTT meta-analyses not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a 'sleep on it' decision advantage; weak.

source: Hassin (2013) 'Yes, it can' principle; Poincare's limits on unconscious calculation, as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Gilhooly argues unconscious work cannot be conscious work minus awareness: long calculations with held intermediate results need working memory. Hassin's principle says unconscious processes can do the same high-level functions; Sklar et al. (2012) showed priming from subliminal two- and three-digit sums, which Gilhooly judges far short of long calculations.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Open dispute, not resolved by the data cited.
agent_relevance: If 'unconscious work' is spreading activation, an LLM already does it inside one forward pass; extra pauses add no new compute type.

source: Helie and Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model, Psychological Review 117:994-1024
finding: Explicit-Implicit Interaction (EII) theory: five principles (explicit and implicit knowledge both exist and differ; both processes usually run together; redundant representation; integration of results; iterative, possibly bidirectional processing). Implemented in the CLARION architecture and used to simulate human data. Helie et al. (2008), via Gilhooly, found more demanding interpolated tasks lowered reminiscence in free recall.
numbers: Abstract-level only; no fit statistics read.
limits: Abstract only. Gilhooly notes the model does not produce a breakthrough into consciousness without an explicit return to the task.
agent_relevance: The one formal model of Wallas's four stages. Links to the Hybrid and connectionist (CLARION) subfield in this run.

source: Nair, Gizzi, Sinapov (2024) Creative Problem Solving in Large Language and Vision Models: What Would it Take? arXiv:2405.01453
finding: Position paper with preliminary experiments. Appendix B describes Wallas's four stages and the Helie and Sun CLARION implementation, and a Gizzi et al. (2022) mapping: preparation = problem formulation, incubation plus illumination = knowledge representation and manipulation, verification = evaluation. States that LLMs are weak at discontinuous Eureka-type tasks.
numbers: Numbers from the experiments were not extracted from the text I read.
limits: No LLM incubation test. Stages are mapped only as a design framework.
agent_relevance: Only a framework mapping; no measured effect of an incubation stage in an LLM.

source: Kumar, Vincentius, Jordan, Anderson (2025) Human Creativity in the Age of LLMs, CHI 2025, arXiv:2410.03703
finding: Two preregistered experiments: LLM help raised performance while on, but did not improve and may have hurt later unassisted creativity. Relevant as evidence on human attempts after exposure to LLM output (an externally supplied prime).
numbers: N = 1,100 (460 divergent AUT, 640 convergent RAT). AUT test originality, strategies vs no LLM H(2) = 9.14, p = 0.010; exposure originality H(2) = 3.78, p = 0.151. RAT test accuracy F(2,1256) = 5.134, p = 0.006; guidance group -10.6 points vs no LLM (95% CI -18.6 to -2.7, p = 0.005); answer group p = 0.682.
quote: may inadvertently hinder independent creative performance when users work without assistance
limits: About humans using an LLM, not LLM incubation. Five AUT objects, short exposure, guidance conditions more verbose.
agent_relevance: Not a test of incubation in a model, but a warning about premature external answers.

source: Polyak and Balkhyoor (2026) Before the Prompt: Heteromorphic Imagination and the Cognitive Cost of Premature Crystallization in Human-AI Co-Creativity, ICCC 2026
finding: Theory paper. Argues that prompt-based AI use forces early linguistic articulation and skips a pre-verbal associative phase, narrowing later ideation. Predicts early-prompt conditions give more fluency but less semantic distance and delayed originality than delayed-prompt conditions, and proposes interfaces with staged incubation.
numbers: No data. Three testable predictions only. Cites Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024): AI images during sketching raised design fixation and cut fluency, variety and originality versus no support.
limits: Untested hypothesis, framed as falsifiable. The neural component is explicitly a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Delaying the answer to keep options open is a human-side design hypothesis, not a result.

source: Macchi, Turco, Inglese, Caravona (2026) The Eyes as a Mirror of the Unconscious: pupil dilation in insight problem solving
finding: Pupil dilation during an arithmetic break was used as a proxy for unconscious effort on insight problems. Eventual solvers kept high and steady pupil dilation throughout incubation, while the other two groups' pupil size fell during the arithmetic.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; pupil size is an indirect marker. Not replicated.
agent_relevance: Supports covert work during breaks; Baird 2012 and Gilhooly argue the work is not intermittent conscious thought.

source: Search note: LLM incubation tests
finding: Searches (Europe PMC, two web searches, one arXiv attempt) found no study that tests a Wallas incubation stage or a delay or distraction step in an LLM and reports a measured effect. The closest items are the position papers above and human-AI studies.
numbers: 0 direct LLM incubation studies found; coverage of arXiv is incomplete because the export API returned empty responses.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search budget; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the schema decision to list incubation as not to add: there is no measured LLM benefit to cite.
